 Six-month-old baby battles life-threatening dengue as lungs, liver and nervous system are affected; survives after intensive care 
 Six-month-old baby battles life-threatening dengue as lungs, liver and nervous system are affected; survives after intensive care 
 TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 05, 2026, 23:44 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print (Representative image) A six-month-old boy who developed severe dengue with life-threatening complications involving the lungs, circulation, liver and nervous system has recovered following intensive care. The infant, admitted on September 21, developed shock, respiratory failure and bleeding, requiring advanced respiratory support and intensive monitoring. He has since made significant clinical improvement and has been discharged. The infant was brought to the hospital with high-grade fever, vomiting, loose stools, poor feeding and reduced urine output. He also experienced a generalised convulsion lasting approximately five to ten minutes, followed by drowsiness. Investigations confirmed dengue infection, with both NS1 antigen and IgM tests positive. Blood tests revealed a low platelet count, hyponatraemia, markedly elevated liver enzymes and abnormalities in blood clotting. As his condition deteriorated, the infant developed respiratory distress and bleeding from the mouth and airway. He was transferred to the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU), intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. With the development of shock and poor circulation, medications were initiated to support blood pressure and organ perfusion. He also required packed red blood cell and fresh frozen plasma transfusions to manage the bleeding and associated complications. Persistent hypoxaemia and airway bleeding necessitated high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), an advanced mode of respiratory support used in selected critically ill patients. Dr Prateek Kataria, Paediatric Intensivist at Manipal Hospitals MomStory, Nagar Road, explained that the infant required close monitoring and escalation of respiratory and circulatory support as his condition evolved. Doctors also suspected cardiac involvement after blood tests showed elevated cardiac markers suggestive of possible myocardial injury. Although echocardiography was normal, the findings prompted close monitoring of cardiac function and appropriate supportive treatment. A further challenge emerged when investigations revealed markedly elevated ferritin levels, raising suspicion of dengue-associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). HLH is a potentially life-threatening hyperinflammatory condition in which excessive immune activation can cause significant organ damage. Early recognition of this complication is important, as it may require specific treatment in addition to supportive management. Commenting on the case, Dr Sagar Lad, Senior Paediatric Intensivist and PICU In-charge at Manipal Hospitals MomStory, Nagar Road, Pune, said, “Severe dengue in infants can be particularly challenging because the illness may progress rapidly and affect multiple organ systems. In this case, the child developed respiratory failure, bleeding and circulatory instability, requiring advanced respiratory support and intensive haemodynamic monitoring. The suspected HLH complication added another layer of complexity. His gradual improvement in breathing, circulation and laboratory parameters was encouraging. This case highlights the importance of early recognition of warning signs, timely intensive care and continuous reassessment of critically ill children.” As the infant responded to treatment, his respiratory support was gradually reduced. He was weaned from high-frequency oscillatory ventilation to non-invasive ventilation, followed by supplemental oxygen, and eventually maintained adequate oxygen saturation on room air. Dr Preeti Lad, Senior Paediatrician at Manipal Hospitals MomStory, Nagar Road, said the infant showed progressive clinical improvement, with better respiratory function and stabilisation of his overall condition. Follow-up investigations demonstrated improvement in several clinical and laboratory parameters, including platelet counts and liver enzyme levels. MRI of the brain and repeat electroencephalography (EEG) were normal. His anti-seizure medication was gradually reduced, and he was transitioned to oral treatment. Dr Santosh Kait, Paediatrician at Manipal Hospitals MomStory, Nagar Road, noted that the child’s clinical progress was encouraging and that continued follow-up would be important following discharge. At discharge, the infant had stable vital signs, was maintaining adequate oxygen levels without respiratory support and was accepting oral feeds. He was discharged with appropriate medical advice and follow-up arrangements. Dr Sagar Lad added, “Dengue-associated HLH is an important and potentially life-threatening complication that clinicians must consider when the clinical course or laboratory findings suggest an exaggerated inflammatory response. Timely recognition and appropriate management are essential to improve outcomes.” What Parents Should Watch for During Dengue
 Dengue can initially resemble other viral infections, with symptoms such as fever, vomiting, reduced appetite and general discomfort. In infants, who cannot communicate their symptoms, changes in feeding, activity and urine output are particularly important indicators. Warning signs requiring prompt medical assessment include:
 •Persistent vomiting or severe abdominal pain. •Bleeding from the nose or gums, or blood in vomit or stools. •Unusual drowsiness, irritability or altered responsiveness. •Breathing difficulty or seizures. •Markedly reduced urine output. •Pale, cold or clammy skin, which may indicate poor circulation. A fall in temperature does not always mean that dengue is resolving. The critical phase may begin around the time the fever subsides, commonly during the first week of illness. During this period, plasma leakage can reduce circulating blood volume and lead to shock. Careful observation remains important even when the fever appears to be improving. Dengue diagnosis depends on clinical assessment and appropriate laboratory investigations, including NS1 antigen or antibody testing according to the stage of illness. Doctors may monitor blood counts, liver function, hydration, urine output and circulation to assess disease severity. Platelet count alone does not determine the severity of dengue or the need for intensive care. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Management focuses on careful fluid administration, close monitoring and timely treatment of complications. Severe cases may require intensive care, respiratory support, blood products when clinically indicated and medicines to support circulation. Fluid management is particularly important because both inadequate and excessive fluid administration can be harmful. The key message for parents is to seek early medical attention if an infant develops fever with poor feeding, reduced urine output or unusual behaviour. Breathing difficulty, significant bleeding, seizures or altered responsiveness require emergency assessment. Early recognition and appropriate medical care can help identify complications and improve the chances of recovery. End of Article Follow Us On Social Media Photostories
